The foundational structure of measure theory is built upon Boolean σ-rings equipped with a positive measure μ. The key innovation lies in redefining equality modulo null sets—two sets E and F are considered equal if their symmetric difference has zero measure. This allows for a consistent definition of measure on equivalence classes, ensuring that μ(E) = μ(F) whenever E = F[μ]. This construction yields a measure ring (S(μ), μ), where S(μ) denotes the σ-ring with this new equality relation. The resulting structure supports isomorphisms between measure rings, preserving both set operations and measure values. These isomorphisms enable the transfer of probabilistic reasoning across equivalent domains, forming the basis for Bayesian inference and state transition modeling in GSI and GSE respectively. The dual nature of this framework—both algebraic (Boolean σ-ring) and measure-theoretic—ensures robustness against singularities and enables formal treatment of probabilistic uncertainty.
